# “Ekip Manman”: Group Prenatal Care Adapted for Pregnant Haitian Immigrants in Boston, Massachusetts

**Authors:** Luca Anna Koritsanszky; Brynn Macaulay; Claire Gonzalez; Kate Mitchell Balla; Katharine Hutchinson; Thamarah Crevecoeur

**Affiliations:** 1Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine at Boston University, Boston Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA. | 2Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA. | 3Birthworker Equity in Education Collaborative at Boston College Connell School of Nursing, Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts, USA. | 4Boston College Connell School of Nursing & Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine, Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts, USA.

## Abstract

Perinatal health disparities disproportionately impact immigrant populations. Recent federal policy changes in the United States increase health risks for Haitian immigrants in the United States. Group prenatal care improves outcomes among vulnerable groups. Perinatal health professionals at a Boston health center adapted the CenteringPregnancy© model to meet the perinatal needs of Haitian immigrants. This article describes the process of adapting CenteringPregnancy© for Haitian immigrant populations.

This quality improvement project used the Model for Improvement framework to guide adaptation of the CenteringPregnancy© model. A non-exhaustive literature review of the CenteringPregnancy© model and thematic analysis of stakeholder interviews with perinatal care team members at the health center (n = 7) and midwives from partner sites (n = 3) informed the adaptation process. Interviews aimed to better understand adverse social determinants of health, the importance of mental health, and the challenges patients face navigating the paradigms of the Haitian and American health care systems. The Salutogenic Framework was used to identify best practices for effective group care that improve comprehensibility, manageability, and meaningfulness for Haitian immigrants.

Five adaptations to the CenteringPregnancy© model emerged from stakeholder interviews: (1) prioritizing mental health, (2) integrating immigration expertise, (3) addressing differing medical paradigms between Haiti and the United States, (4) building early bridges to pediatric care, and (5) reducing social isolation. Educational materials were also developed in Haitian Creole.

Factors for successful implementation included institutional buy-in, integration of a perinatal care coordinator, adjunct routine obstetric care for high-risk pregnancies, scalable electronic medical record systems, and ongoing care coordination across the care team.

“Ekip Manman,” the adapted group care model, advances maternal health equity for Haitian immigrants in Boston. This adaptation can inform culturally tailored perinatal programs for other immigrant communities in Boston and beyond—and can contribute to perinatal health equity efforts throughout the United States.

Keywords: CenteringPregnancy, community health center, group prenatal care, Haitian, Haiti, health disparities, health equity, immigrant, maternal health, perinatal health, pregnancy

## Background

In 2024, an estimated 701,570 Haitian immigrants were living in the United States. 1 Natural disasters, political instability, poverty, and family reunification have driven migration to the United States. The assassination of the Haitian president in 2021 followed by worsening political instability, escalating gang violence, and shifting immigration policies in Chile and Brazil, which had previously welcomed Haitians, have resulted in an increase in Haitian immigration to the United States. 2 Boston, Massachusetts (MA) is home to the third largest diaspora of Haitians in the United States, totaling 55,000 immigrants in 2021. 2

Improving perinatal outcomes among immigrant populations is essential to advancing maternal health equity in the United States.3–6 The Haitian immigrant population experiences multifaceted barriers to reproductive health care and worse perinatal outcomes than their counterparts born in the United States.7–11 Studies of immigrants from low- and middle-income countries to Western nations have identified communication, cultural and language misunderstanding between patients and clinicians; suboptimal care quality; difficulty navigating the health care system in a new country; and poor treatment by health providers as factors preventing improvements in perinatal health outcomes.12–16 Additionally, fear of deportation, which is worsening as the Trump administration recently succeeded in ending the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) program for Haitians, and competing priorities such as the need to secure housing, food, and employment present additional barriers to prenatal care utilization.16–18

Refugee populations experience higher rates of stillbirth, surgical birth, preterm birth, low birth weight, inadequate prenatal care, and lower rates of exclusive breastfeeding.7–11,19 A recent study revealed that 43% of refugees and asylum seekers did not visit a health care provider in the year before pregnancy, compared to 27% of U.S.-born women. 20 Haitian birthing people in MA face heightened health risks, including one of the highest rates of gestational diabetes (13%) and an increased likelihood of late preterm birth. 21 Compared to their counterparts who immigrated to the United States prior to 2021, recently arrived Haitian immigrants experience an elevated prevalence of hypertensive diseases (60% vs. 24%) and postpartum financial insecurity (47% vs. 12%). 22 Pregnancy and postpartum experiences among immigrants are often compounded by past trauma, cultural conflicts between their traditions and those of the host country, social isolation, and mental health issues such as higher rates of perinatal depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder.9,23–27 Rising fears of deportation have contributed to growing mental distress and increased risk of poor mental health outcomes among Haitian immigrants.28,29

Several large studies have demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in preterm birth among Black pregnant people enrolled in group prenatal care.30–41 Group prenatal care increases breastfeeding initiation and exclusive breastfeeding, particularly among Black and Hispanic women.32,34–36 Group prenatal care has also been shown to improve psychosocial functioning and reduce perinatal depression, stress, and anxiety among vulnerable and socially isolated women. 42 While group prenatal care models such as CenteringPregnancy© have not consistently demonstrated efficacy in improving health outcomes for all populations,30–33,43–45 several studies demonstrate significant results when stratified by vulnerability indicators.33–35,44 These results point to the potential for group prenatal care to improve outcomes among Black, Hispanic, immigrant, and low-income birthing people.

CenteringPregnancy© has been shown to increase prenatal and postpartum visit attendance, including among immigrants.42,46,47 Among low-income Black and Hispanic patients, group prenatal care models are associated with increased patient satisfaction with health care, prenatal knowledge, and self-reported readiness for childbirth.34–36,48,49 Improving patient experience is especially important among vulnerable populations, as these populations are more likely to experience discrimination and trauma in their care experiences. 50

While group prenatal care is an appealing model to meet the needs of Haitian pregnant people, the CenteringPregnancy© curriculum requires adaptation and reimagination to be culturally and linguistically responsive to the needs of the population. This article describes the authors’ process for adapting and reimagining the CenteringPregnancy© model into “Ekip Manman,” to meet the needs of the Haitian immigrant population at a Federally Qualified Health Center (FQHC) in Boston, MA. The authors looked to the Model for Improvement (MFI) framework to guide this quality improvement (QI) project and the Salutogenic Framework to enhance cultural responsiveness, social support, and engagement with care. 51 The article also describes the specific changes to the model and shares considerations for implementation.

## Methods

### Overview of quality improvement initiative

This project was conducted as a QI initiative aimed at adapting the CenteringPregnancy© group prenatal care model to better meet the needs of Haitian immigrant patients receiving care at a FQHC in Boston, MA. It was guided by principles from the MFI, which emphasizes iterative adaptation of care processes based on local context and stakeholder input. 52 The project focused on identifying gaps in engagement among Haitian immigrant patients and modifying the structure and curriculum of CenteringPregnancy© to better address cultural, linguistic, and social needs. Initial adaptations were informed by literature review, consultation with stakeholders, and ongoing collaboration among the interdisciplinary care team.

### Ethical approval

Institutional Review Board approval was not required for the process of adapting CenteringPregnancy© because this work was classified as an informal QI initiative and was conducted in accordance with all applicable institutional policies and procedures for QI activities at the FQHC.

### Implementation site

This adaptation project was conducted at a FQHC in an underserved Boston neighborhood with a large Haitian community. 53 Many patients live below the Federal Poverty Line and are insured through MassHealth. 54 The FQHC serves as a primary care provider for Haitian immigrants and has prior experience implementing CenteringPregnancy©; this project supported the relaunch of group prenatal care following its suspension during the COVID-19 pandemic.

In January 2025, the FQHC partnered with a local university with funding from the MA Department of Public Health to adapt group prenatal care for pregnant Haitian immigrants and establish a clinical excellence training site for community-based group prenatal care. The partnership aimed to improve patient experience, social cohesion, and care engagement—including postpartum transition to primary care—while advancing outcomes often associated with CenteringPregnancy© such as reducing low birth weight and increasing breastfeeding.

### Framework for adaptation: salutogenesis

We employed Aaron Antonovsky’s Salutogenic Framework of health as a foundation to guide the adaptation of the CenteringPregnancy© model. Salutogenesis shifts focus from the traditional pathogenic orientation—“what causes disease?” – to ask, “What promotes health?”. 55 Central to this model is the concept of a sense of coherence, defined as: an individual’s enduring confidence that their life is comprehensible (that events and demands in their lives are structured, predictable, and understandable rather than chaotic), manageable (to support individuals in feeling that they have both internal and external resources to effectively cope with stressors), and meaningful (to promote that life’s challenges are worthy of investment). We applied the salutogenic lens to identify and reinforce cultural and community-based assets that could strengthen Haitian immigrants’ capacity to manage the stressors of pregnancy, migration, and systemic marginalization. By framing health as a dynamic process emerging from the interaction between individuals and their social environments, the Salutogenic Framework offered a culturally resonant, strengths-based framework for this adaptation.

### Overall methodology for adapting the CenteringPregnancy© model

The authors used an informal, QI approach to adapt the CenteringPregnancy© model that integrated three sources of information. We began by (1) reviewing the CenteringPregnancy© curriculum and facilitators’ guide to increase our understanding of the structure, format, and educational content of each session. 56 This was followed by (2) a review of relevant literature using Harvard Hollis, Harvard University’s academic search engine and repository of academic writing, to further understand the implementation of CenteringPregnancy© across diverse populations and their clinical and psychosocial outcomes, with particular attention to its implementation among immigrant and low-income communities. Through this search, we created a non-exhaustive database of publications examining group-based prenatal care implementation and outcomes. Finally, we (3) conducted semi-structured interviews with local experts in the delivery of group prenatal care and perinatal health care for newcomers to the Boston area to learn more about success factors from local efforts.

### Data collection

Semi-structured interviews were conducted with experts to identify challenges, elicit best practices, and understand systems-level factors relating to coordination of care across a complex health care system. Key stakeholders were identified by their current or former professional roles in the provision of group-based prenatal care and who are established experts in migrant and refugee maternal health in the Boston area. Snowball sampling was used to identify additional stakeholders with relevant clinical and system-level experience. Within the FQHC, we interviewed a Haitian-American Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM) who has 15 years experience caring for this population, two patient care coordinators who are experienced in facilitating group prenatal care, two behavioral health specialists, a pediatrician, one clinical operations specialist, and the FQHC’s Director of Clinical Services and Population Health. Most of these health professionals are members of the Haitian community. Next, we interviewed three CNMs who provide maternity care at the Immigrant and Refugee Health Center at Boston Medical Center. Finally, we interviewed the Neighborhood Birth Center (NBC) team who developed and adapted an empowered birth education workshop for Haitian immigrants. These interviews lasted 45–60 min and were not recorded given the QI nature of this project. One interviewer took notes and relevant quotations during the interviews.

### Data analysis

Stakeholder interview notes were analyzed using an iterative approach to thematic analysis to identify recurring themes relating to gaps in care, service coordination, and social determinants of health affecting prenatal care engagement among Haitian immigrants. All notes were reviewed and analyzed by two members of the team and a consensus driven process was achieved through regular QI meetings to discuss findings and identify major overarching themes. Major themes were linked to the QI MFI and triangulated with the core components of the CenteringPregnancy© model using the Salutogenic Framework to identify strategies to support group antenatal care that enhance participants’ experiences of comprehensibility, manageability, and meaningfulness, as well as infrastructure and system changes required to support implementation. Our methods were guided by a commitment to designing a care model that enhances health equity and mobilizes intrinsic and extrinsic resources to promote well-being in a population for whom social isolation, displacement, and systemic exclusion pose profound threats to perinatal health.

## Results

Data analysis from our stakeholder interviews revealed three major themes: (1) Significant adverse social determinants, (2) The importance of mental health, and (3) Challenges that Haitian pregnant people face navigating the differences between Haitian and American health care paradigms. These results provided valuable recommendations for adaptation of (1) the curriculum, (2) the provision of wrap-around support services for this complex high-risk population throughout group care implementation, and (3) bridging of mental health and pediatric care.

A common recommendation that emerged from the interviews was the need to adapt the CenteringPregnancy© model to address the social determinants of health that affect Haitian immigrants. Social needs such as unstable housing and food insecurity were identified as immediate concerns. Stakeholders described how these pressures shape patients’ day-to-day realities, often making it difficult for pregnant individuals to prioritize or consistently engage in prenatal care. One interviewee stressed the importance of incorporating social and case workers into group prenatal care so that “patients can get answers [to urgent needs] in real time.”

However, the same interviewee cautioned against over-promising or failure to disclose the limitations of the prenatal care program. “Many times, the expectations of the patients [are] that ‘I’m going to get housing.’” For this reason there must be explicit communication about the scope of the group prenatal care model in order to prevent misunderstandings that erode trust between patients and providers.

Second, stakeholders underscored the importance of mental health. Stakeholders described how many patients arrive in the United States carrying trauma from migration journeys, political instability, and family separation. These experiences are often reflected in patients’ described reports of loneliness and emotional distress during pregnancy. They are often separated from key support people, including parents, partners, and children—and disclose feelings of isolation in the United States. Interviewees identified the potential for group prenatal care to reduce social isolation. One interviewee noted: “[There is a] social side [to] having another group of women who look like them and talk like them…[because] they’re so alone.”

The third theme highlighted challenges that Haitian pregnant people face in navigating the stark differences between Haitian and American paradigms of medicine. Many Haitian women prefer to use natural and herbal remedies to treat ailments and illnesses, which they may not initially disclose to United States health care providers.57,58 One interviewee expressed how the social nature and shared experience of group prenatal care “help[s] facilitate trust with providers over time”, which may lead to more open discussion between patients and providers.

Finally, experts identified difficulties navigating insurance enrollment, lack of appropriate interpretation services, and exposure to a high-intensity medical system, which can lead to overwhelm and distrust. 57 One clinician acknowledged “So many of our patients have the same questions, same concerns, same knowledge needs.”

### Comprehensibility: navigation challenges of the american health care paradigm

Curriculum adaptations aimed to enhance understanding of pregnancy, birth, and early parenting within the U.S. health care context while honoring Haitian culture and the newcomer experience address Haitian patient’s challenges with navigating the different paradigms of the Haitian and American health care system. Building on CenteringPregnancy©’s participant-driven model, Ekip Manman’s sessions integrated Haitian perinatal practices and non-biomedical perspectives alongside United States pregnancy care.

A key adaptation was that, in each session, facilitators sought to create space for participants to reflect, share, and integrate traditional knowledge alongside biomedical care. Additionally, we partnered with NBC to include an Empowered Birth workshop, delivered by culturally and linguistically congruent birth workers. Through interactive case scenarios, this session expanded CenteringPregnancy©’s focus on labor and birth, familiarizing participants with United States labor and delivery settings, care teams, labor management practices, decision-making processes, and power dynamics—promoting autonomy and alignment between participants’ values and care expectations in order to reduce the risk of birth trauma.

While CenteringPregnancy© requires facilitator continuity, our adaptation further required cultural and linguistic concordance: the core facilitation team identifies as Haitian ethnically and is Haitian Creole-speaking, supporting comprehensibility and ongoing cultural adaptation across sessions.

### Manageability: importance of mental health & adverse social determinants of health

In contrast to the traditional CenteringPregnancy© model, which focuses primarily on prenatal care delivery and facilitating participant discussion, the Ekip Manman model sought to increase participants’ capacity to navigate pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period by strengthening practical support and care continuity. These additional supports include embedded behavioral health, pediatric care, and a supported transition to primary care in the postpartum period, as well as non-clinical supports with immigration-specific needs. This adaptation not only addresses the importance of mental health but also takes into account adverse social determinants of health affecting health care, such as the various challenges associated with immigration.

While CenteringPregnancy© addresses psychosocial topics primarily through facilitated discussion and referral, Ekip Manman integrates behavioral health services directly into group care as a single behavioral health provider attends four sessions (two prenatally, two in the postpartum period), with telemedicine follow-up providing flexibility and responsiveness to emerging needs. This strategy seeks to normalize behavioral health care in a population where there is significant stigma surrounding mental health. In addition to the standard CenteringPregnancy© curriculum components, we include newcomer-relevant discussions like transitioning to parenting while simultaneously navigating challenges relating to immigration.

Unlike Centering Pregnancy©, which focuses primarily on prenatal and intrapartum preparation, Ekip Manman incorporates two pediatrician-led sessions addressing newborn care norms during hospitalization and the first month of life to prepare participants with an understanding of neonatal care practices in the United States, with the aim of empowering birthing parents to make clinical decisions for their newborns. The same pediatric health care provider then returns for two postpartum dyad sessions at 6 weeks and 4 months to promote engagement with pediatric care upon graduation from the group.

Recognizing that immigration-related stressors fall outside the scope of standard prenatal education, the model added a dedicated group session with an immigration specialist to address participants’ legal and system-navigation questions.

Traditional CenteringPregnancy© implementation often excludes individuals who require higher-acuity obstetric care. Given the large proportion of Haitian immigrant patients at the FQHC who carry a medically high-risk diagnosis, we’ve established a mechanism for co-management with an obstetrician or maternal-fetal medicine specialist, allowing participants who would otherwise be recommended transfer of care to join sessions and benefit from the salutogenic components of this group model while also receiving indicated specialty oversight.

### Meaningfulness: importance of mental health & navigation challenges of the american health care paradigm

Given that many Haitian new arrivals are at risk for adverse mental health outcomes and poor maternity care experiences, the adaptation of integrating culturally congruent doulas into the group prenatal care model addresses patients’ challenges navigating the American health system while promoting improved mental health outcomes through social support and reducing isolation. 59 While traditional CenteringPregnancy© models emphasize participant engagement and shared experience, Ekip Manman explicitly centered participants’ cultural identities, values, and lived experiences as a core driver of curriculum design and group structure. The collectivism of Haitian culture was honored by ensuring that cohorts were clustered by gestational age, ethnicity, and newcomer status to reflect shared migration experiences and strengthen collective meaning-making.

We partnered with Dottapan Doulas (DD) to ensure all patients are supported by a familiar individual at the time of delivery and throughout the postpartum period. DD is a community doula collaborative that convenes trained multicultural doulas, including those of Haitian descent, who are concurrently trained as community health workers (CHWs) and support their clients to navigate community resources. These services are reimbursable through MA Medicaid. This partnership extends collectivism beyond the standard CenteringPregnancy© support structures by incorporating known individuals who are to be present for labor through immediate postpartum support in the inpatient practice setting where midwifery and provider care continuity is not guaranteed.

Although the traditional CenteringPregnancy© model emphasizes experiential and discussion-based learning over written materials, Ekip Manman supplemented group sessions with approximately 30 easy-to-read, Creole-language handouts to support understanding and reinforce meaning beyond the group setting.

Appendix A1 provides a detailed overview of per-session adaptations that were made to create the Ekip Manman model.

## Discussion

Our reimagination of the CenteringPregnancy© model, Ekip Manman, amplifies the strengths of Haitian culture and prioritizes factors that promote health—physically, socially, and mentally. These adaptations are driven by the Salutogenic Framework’s central ideas of promoting a sense of cohesion by making life more comprehensible, manageable, and meaningful.

Implementing this model required structural and operational redesign at the health center to integrate it into routine FQHC activities. Because addressing perinatal health inequities among vulnerable populations is an institutional priority, the FQHC leadership provided essential and sustained support and buy-in for Ekip Manman. This commitment enabled successful implementation, including QI processes, operational changes such as scheduling and staff training and supervision.

A central innovation was the introduction of a perinatal care coordinator (PCC), a Haitian Creole-speaking, credentialed CHW who bridges clinical and community settings to provide culturally congruent support. The PCC’s role includes group organization (i.e., scheduling and appointment reminder calls), care coordination, meetings with patients to assess social determinant needs, and offer community based resources to ensure that participants have newborn essentials (i.e., carseat, breast pumps, diapers, and a safe place to sleep). Their role is essential for successful implementation, involving patient recruitment and retention, co-facilitation of group sessions, and CHW-oriented work (i.e., screening and referrals to community resources). Furthermore, Ekip Manman requires a structured, interdisciplinary approach with regular meetings to allow for collaborative debriefing, anchored by the PCC.

Ekip Manman was designed to integrate pediatric care and behavioral health early and promote continuity beyond birth by including these specialists in two prenatal group sessions and two postpartum sessions to provide dyad care, in addition to routinely scheduled newborn visits. This approach aims to reduce care fragmentation with interdisciplinary partners, enabling earlier identification of maternal mental health and social challenges, 42 and has been shown in other settings to improve patient satisfaction,35,48,60 newborn and primary care visit attendance,33,49,60 breastfeeding rates34–36,49 and contraceptive uptake. 61

The expert interviews provided an opportunity for the FQHC to develop partnerships with other community organizations. For example, the DD were incorporated into our adapted group prenatal care model to provide psychological support to Haitian immigrants prenatally, during labor, and postpartum. Additionally, the NBC and the FQHC identified a shared mission to center, protect, and uplift marginalized patient populations, through which we formed a partnership of knowledge exchange, sharing of ideas, and mutual institutional support. These partnerships were critical for the implementation of Ekip Manman and pave the way for future collaborations that will support the well-being of immigrants in Boston.

While Ekip Manman was developed within a well-resourced FQHC with strong institutional support, several core elements of the model are adaptable to other settings serving immigrant populations. Core elements such as culturally and linguistically concordant group facilitation and curriculum adaptations that integrate participants’ health beliefs, migration experience, and community knowledge allow the model to be tailored to local populations. Where implementing sites are limited on internal capacity to make these adaptations, they can leverage partnership with community-based organizations, who can support culturally responsive curriculum development.

We designed Ekip Manman with an eye toward scalability across health care settings. The core structure of group prenatal care provides the operational blueprint for implementation and has been shown in prior studies to be feasible in diverse clinical environments. In our model, the integration of pediatric, behavioral health, and family medicine providers expands this blueprint beyond obstetric care to support dyadic and family-centered care. While we believe that these elements strengthen care continuity, they may be implemented flexibly depending on available resources.

In July 2025, the authors received additional funding to study implementation of Ekip Manman from the perspectives of birthing people and care teams. We anticipate that this study will yield valuable information relating to the acceptability and experience of the Ekip Manman program from patient and provider perspectives—as well as implementation insights to inform further adaptations and scale-up in other communities. These findings will be shared in a future publication.

## Limitations

A key limitation of this work is that, as a QI initiative, interviews were limited to health system and community stakeholders. Patient engagement was beyond the scope of this phase, as it would have required research oversight and ethical approval, but will be incorporated in a subsequent funded implementation trial through structured end-of-cohort feedback. Although patients were not interviewed directly during this initial QI project, many stakeholders interviewed were clinicians and community members who shared a linguistic and cultural background with participants and brought extensive experience caring for Haitian immigrant patients. Additionally, reliance on grant funding—primarily to support provider and nursing time—may limit replication in community health centers without external funding.

## Conclusion and Health Equity Implications

There is no other time in a person’s life, outside of serious illness, when engagement with the health care system is as intensive as during pregnancy. The perinatal period offers a unique opportunity to promote health and health-seeking behaviors among populations with high burdens of chronic and infectious disease, behavioral health needs, and resource insecurity. Ekip Manman illustrates how equity-centered design can transform perinatal systems by redistributing clinical and social support to communities most affected by structural exclusion. It offers an evidence-based approach to addressing profound perinatal health disparities among Haitian immigrant and refugee populations in Boston, while enabling limited resources to be concentrated across a larger group of high-need patients. Through culturally responsive, community-embedded strategies, Ekip Manman advances broader public health goals of equity, access, health promotion, and social inclusion. The model is adaptable across health centers, community hospitals, and tertiary care settings. Sustained investment in interdisciplinary collaboration, evaluation, and policy advocacy will be critical to expanding its impact locally, regionally, and nationally.
